doc.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007

title: Working with R&B studio players and growing up as a young producer
summary: Dorn paired Fathead with R&B rhythm players like Bernard Purdie and Richard Tee. He never forced anyone and learned on the job at about 20, helped by King Curtis.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: So do you say to him, because you’re not a composer —
I’m not an anything. Use that as a gauge.
Okay. So what do you say to him as far as the tunes? You say Fathead, what do you got here that —

Well it varies from artist to artist. With David, he was open to me suggesting songs and he also listened to the radio so he didn’t just listen to jazz. So he was open. And when I started saying I don’t want to work with like jazz rhythm sections, I want to work with R&B studio cats like Bernard Purdie and Richard Tee and Eric Gale and Chuck Rainey. I want to work with those guys. But they had a very high level of musicianship beyond just, you know, playing on commercial records. The guys could play. So when they got with jazz guys it gave them a chance to stretch a little, or sometimes stretch a lot. And so I would tell David, well here’s what I want to do. Or he would tell me here’s what he wants to do, and we’d meet. If I gave him a song if he dug it he’d play it. I never forced anybody. First of all I couldn’t, I was a child. These were men. So I couldn’t force anybody to do anything and I never would. It’s not a comfortable way to go. But as I started doing these and they started working, guys were more open to doing stuff like

that. And also jazz radio at that time, listen I played Lady and Trane and Miles and Prez and you know like Ellington and Mingus, all that stuff. But the thrust of my show was the popular jazz of the day: Horace and Cannon and Blakey and you know, whoever had like a jazz hit or whoever had albums that went beyond the three, four, five thousand selling jazz records.
Did you ever butt heads with Bernard Purdie?

No. One time you know he stopped a take and I got pissed. But I got along with the guys you know. First of all I was a child producer I’m telling you. I started producing when I was like 20. So all these guys were older than me. And it was kind of, I kind of grew up in the studio with them you know? Like King Curtis was a great friend and he helped me a lot, he hipped me to a lot of stuff. I mean I always describe myself in those days as having one foot in hip and the other foot in huh, because I really didn’t know. I was like hipper than the average idiot but not hip enough to know what I was doing. You know it was an odd spot. I was really learning on the fly. So when I called myself a producer with training wheels I really mean it. I kind of learned on the job and then all of a sudden, you know, I just caught a wave for like ten years.
